sections.title: Attributing a Stain: To Whom, at What Cost, on What Surface
sections.gist: The first Mishnah and its Gemara: which gentile qualifies, a borrower who would lose less than the lender, a borrower impure only from her own stain, and R. Nechemia's rule for surfaces not susceptible to impurity.

children.title: Mishnah: Lent Garment, Shared Bench, Stone Bench
children.gist: A lender attributes a stain to a gentile or *niddah* borrower; three women who shared a garment or bench are all impure; R. Nechemia rules them pure on a surface not susceptible to *tumah*.

bullets.text: A woman lent her garment to a gentile or to a *niddah*, then wore it and found a stain: she attributes it to the borrower (*tolah bah*).

Earlier cases of *teliyah* (the butcher, the husband's nosebleed, a wound) blamed a source that loses nothing. Here the stain is pinned on another woman, and it costs these borrowers nothing: the *niddah* is already *teme'ah*, and a gentile is not bound by the laws of *niddah*.
No greater likelihood that the stain is the borrower's is required. Since no one loses, the lenient attribution is taken, in keeping with the rabbinic character of *ketamim*.
Three women wore one garment or sat on one bench (*safsal*) in turn. It was checked clean before the first, and a stain was found after the third: all three are *teme'ot*.

No woman is a better candidate than the others, so none can shift the stain onto another. Compare two travelers on two paths, one over a buried corpse: each asking alone is *tahor*, but both together cannot be declared pure.
If they sat on a stone bench or a bathhouse bench (*itzteva*, fixed to the floor), R. Nechemia rules all three *tehorot*: anything not susceptible to *tumah* is not susceptible to *ketamim*.

Tosafot: stain law is built on the impurity of the object. If the object cannot become *tamei*, the chain never reaches the woman. This makes laws of *kelim* (such as whether synthetic materials can become *tamei*) essential for *hilkhot niddah* today.

children.title: Which Gentile? Seen Blood, Fit to See, or Any at All
children.gist: Rav limits the Mishnah to a gentile who has already menstruated. Rav Sheshet calls this an error from a baraita, and Rava rereads that baraita so that Rav follows the first tanna.

bullets.text: Rav: the Mishnah means a gentile woman of age who has already had a flow. He learns it from the pairing with *niddah*: just as a *niddah* is one who sees, so is the gentile.

Rav Sheshet: Rav said this while dozing. A baraita says she attributes the stain to a gentile, and R. Meir says only to one fit to see. So the first tanna allows any gentile, and even R. Meir asks only that she be fit to see, not that she has actually bled.
Rava: why assume R. Meir is being strict? He is lenient. Another baraita: she may not attribute to a gentile, and R. Meir says she may.
Read together: the first tanna allows only a gentile who has actually seen blood, and R. Meir allows one merely fit to see, even if she has never bled. Rav follows the first tanna.
So attribution needs more than "no one loses": it must not be implausible. The two tanna'im differ only on how much of a record the gentile needs.

rows: Any gentile woman, whatever her age
Only a gentile who has already seen blood (as Rav)
Only one fit to see: the stricter view
Even one merely fit to see: the more lenient view

children.title: When the Borrower Would Also Lose: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel vs. Rebbi
children.gist: A borrower who would lose less than the lender: the baraita's dispute, why each side says "therefore", and the extension to two travelers on two paths by Rav Chisda, Rav Adda and R. Yosei son of R. Chanina.

children.title: Shomeret Yom and Soferet Shivah: Blame the Lesser Loss, or Both Impure?
children.gist: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel lets the lender attribute to a borrower who loses less; Rebbi does not, so both are impure; both agree where the borrower loses nothing.

bullets.text: Baraita: the lender may attribute the stain to a *shomeret yom ke'neged yom* on her second day. She has no presumption of bleeding, but her source is considered open.
Likewise to a *soferet shivah* who has not yet immersed, who must now count seven days again.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: therefore the lender is set right and the borrower is spoiled.
Rebbi (R. Yehuda HaNasi): she may not attribute to either; therefore both are spoiled, and both are *teme'ot*.

The loss is lopsided. The lender would face a full *niddah* count, the *shomeret yom* only one more day, and the *soferet shivah* was not yet *tehorah* anyway. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel lets the smaller loss absorb the stain; for Rebbi any real loss rules out attribution.

Both agree she may attribute to a *shomeret yom* on her first day, since she becomes pure the next day either way; to a woman in her days of *dam tohar* after childbirth; and to a virgin at first intercourse, whose blood is presumed hymenal.

chart.caption: Attributing to a borrower: where the two tanna'im part
columns: *Shomeret yom* on her first day; *dam tohar*; virgin

children.title: Why Each Side Says 'Therefore' (Lefikakh)
children.gist: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's "therefore" only mirrors Rebbi's; Rebbi's rules out blaming only the woman who was wearing the garment when the stain was found.

bullets.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's "therefore" adds nothing; the baraita says it to match Rebbi's.
Rebbi's is needed: one might think only the woman wearing the garment when the stain was found is spoiled, not the other. "Therefore" teaches that both are *teme'ot*.
Once attribution fails, no fallback rule, such as who held the garment at the moment of discovery, chooses between them.

children.title: Two Travelers, Two Paths: The Same Dispute? Rav Chisda vs. Rav Adda
children.gist: Rav Chisda ties an impure and a pure traveler on two paths to the same dispute; Rav Adda says even Rebbi would attribute there, since the impure one loses nothing.

bullets.text: Rav Chisda: one *tamei* and one *tahor* walked two paths, one *tamei* from a buried corpse; neither remembers which he took, and afterward they handled *terumah* or *kodashim*. This is the Rebbi–Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dispute: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel assigns the impure path to the one already *tamei*, and Rebbi does not.

Rav Adda objects: perhaps Rebbi spoke only of the *shomeret yom*, who can immerse at any time, so the two women are alike. But the traveler already *tamei* stays *tamei*; what difference does it make to him? There even Rebbi would attribute.
Rav Chisda: the *shomeret yom* too is not fully pure, since she still needs immersion, and yet Rebbi won't attribute to her. So the cases are comparable.
At issue is why Rebbi refuses: because any loss to the other party rules it out, or only because the two parties stand essentially equal.
Tosafot: Rav Chisda's case can't be a traveler who became *tamei* only today, since then even Rebbi would attribute; he must already be partway through his purification.

children.title: R. Yosei son of R. Chanina: Blame the Impure, Even the Doubtful
children.gist: All agree that the impure path goes to the one already impure, even if he is only doubtfully impure, which bears out Rav Adda.

bullets.text: R. Yosei son of R. Chanina: a *tamei* and a *tahor*, or even a *tahor* and a *talui* (impure by doubt), on two paths. The impure path is assigned to the *talui* and the pure path to the *tahor*.
Everyone agrees, Rebbi included. This follows Rav Adda, not Rav Chisda.
The *talui* must treat himself as *tamei* anyway, so the attribution costs him nothing more.

returns_to.note: Decides between Rav Chisda and Rav Adda

children.title: Ketem be'Ketem: Blaming a Woman Impure Only by Her Own Stain
children.gist: R. Yochanan asks whether a stain may be pinned on a woman impure only through a stain; R. Yehuda bar Livai says no. A baraita that seems to say both is reconciled three ways, and Ravina rereads it.

children.title: R. Yochanan's Question: Blood From Her Body, or Perhaps From Outside?
children.gist: The question only arises for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and R. Yehuda bar Livai answers that she may not attribute, since the other woman's stain may itself have an outside source.

bullets.text: R. Yochanan asks R. Yehuda bar Livai: may a stain be attributed to a woman already *teme'ah* because of a *ketem*?
Not according to Rebbi: he won't attribute even to a *shomeret yom*, who saw from her own body, so surely not to one whose impurity may have come from outside.
The question is for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Perhaps he attributes only to a woman who saw from her body, and not to one whose stain may be external; or perhaps there is no difference.
R. Yehuda bar Livai: she may not attribute it, and both are *teme'ot*. The reason: the other woman's earlier stain may itself have come from outside.
On the face of it the other woman loses nothing, since she is impure anyway. The hesitation is whether a woman known only by a stain counts as a real source of bleeding.

children.title: A Baraita at Odds With Itself: Two Tanna'im, Two Days, or Past vs. Future
children.gist: A baraita both rules out and allows attributing to a woman with a stain. It is reconciled as Rebbi against Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, as Rebbi on her first vs. second day, or (Rav Ashi) as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on the past vs. the future.

bullets.text: R. Yochanan objects from a baraita: she may not attribute to a woman impure from a stain; but if she lent to a gentile or to a woman observing days of impurity from a stain, she may.
The baraita contradicts itself. First answer: the first clause is Rebbi, the latter Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

Some say both clauses are Rebbi. She may attribute on the other woman's first day, when she is impure that day anyway, but not on her second day, when she only needs immersion and would lose an extra day.

Rav Ashi: both are Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. The latter clause concerns the past: pure items the other woman already touched were impure anyway. The first concerns her future, where the stain would ruin her count of clean days.
The distinction is formal, not evidentiary: attribution may settle what already happened, but it may not reshape a woman's status going forward.

chart.caption: Three ways to reconcile the baraita on attributing to a woman with a stain
columns: First clause: she may not attribute
rows: Rebbi: the other woman's second day
Rebbi: the other woman's first day
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: her future count
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: items she already touched

children.title: Ravina: The Baraita Means a Gentile or Dam Tohar, Not a Stain
children.gist: Every answer still has Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel attributing to a woman with a stain, against R. Yehuda bar Livai, so Ravina rereads the latter clause as a gentile or a woman in *dam tohar*.

bullets.text: The baraita is settled, but on every answer Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel attributes to a woman with a stain, which is difficult for R. Yehuda bar Livai.
Ravina: the latter clause means that if she lent to a gentile, then as to whether the lender counts as one who saw a stain, she attributes it to the gentile.
But it says "or to a woman observing days of a stain"! Ravina reads it as a woman observing *dam tohar*: she attributes to either, and the lender remains *tehorah*.
So the rule stands: a stain is never attributed to a woman whose only claim is a stain of her own; each permitted case has another basis.

returns_to.note: Defends R. Yehuda bar Livai's answer

children.title: R. Nechemia: No Tumah, No Ketem: Source, Scope, Halakha
children.gist: The verse behind R. Nechemia, its reach to a pot's exterior and tiny rags, and whether the *halakha* follows him, given a case where the Sages ruled both women impure.

children.title: The Ground, a Pot's Outside, a Tiny Rag
children.gist: Rav Mattana gives the verse; Rav Huna and R. Chanina extend it to the outside of an earthenware vessel, and Abaye to rags under three by three fingerbreadths.

bullets.text: Rav Mattana: "and clean she shall sit upon the ground" (Yeshayahu 3:26). Sitting on the ground, which cannot become impure, she is clean.
Rav Huna in the name of R. Chanina: R. Nechemia rules her pure even on the outside of an inverted earthenware vessel, which becomes impure only through its airspace.
Isn't that obvious? It needs saying: one might think the Sages decreed the outside like the inside. There is no such decree.
Abaye: likewise on rags smaller than three by three fingerbreadths, which are of use to neither the poor nor the rich.
What counts is whether this surface or item is *mekabel tumah*, not whether the material generally can become *tamei*.

The three leniencies of *ketamim* (larger than a *geris*, on something *mekabel tumah*, and, in a later Mishnah, on uncolored garments) match the criteria for *nega'im* on garments. This raises the question whether stain law follows formal rules or practical reasoning.

children.title: Halakha Like R. Nechemia? The Hand Mill, the Bathtub, the Olive Leaf
children.gist: Rav rules like R. Nechemia; Rav Nachman objects from a baraita where the Sages ruled both women impure; the answer is a dispute of tanna'im, and the Sages ruled like R. Nechemia.

bullets.text: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Mattana in the name of Rav: the *halakha* follows R. Nechemia.
Rav Nachman: Father teaches of a case of two women whose stain was on something not susceptible to impurity, and the Sages ruled both impure.

The baraita: two women grinding at a hand mill. Blood under the inner woman: both are impure, since the outer one leans in toward the mill. Under the outer woman: she is impure and the inner one pure. Between them: both are impure.
The incidents: blood on the rim of a bathtub, and on an olive leaf while the women fired the oven. The Sages ruled both impure, against R. Nechemia.
Answer: it is a dispute of tanna'im. A baraita: on something not susceptible to impurity, R. Ya'akov rules her impure and R. Nechemia pure, and the Sages ruled like R. Nechemia.

sections.title: Three Women in One Bed: All Impure, One Who Checked, Attributing to Each Other
sections.gist: The next Mishnah; Rav's condition that the woman who checked did so at once, set against Bar Padda's and R. Oshaya's views on timing; and the baraita on which woman may attribute to which.

children.title: Mishnah: All Impure, Unless One Checked or One Is Unfit to See
children.gist: Blood under one of three sleeping women makes all impure, unless one checks and finds herself impure; otherwise they attribute to each other, and if none was fit to see they are treated as fit.

bullets.text: Three women sleeping in one bed, and blood is found under one: all three are *teme'ot*.
They may have shifted in their sleep, so where the blood lies proves nothing.
If one checked herself when the blood was found and found herself impure, she is *teme'ah* and the other two are *tehorot*.
Otherwise they attribute to each other (*tolot zo ba'zo*): one unfit to menstruate, such as a pregnant woman, attributes the blood to those who are fit.
If none of the three was fit to see, they are treated as though fit, and all are *teme'ot*, since the blood came from one of them.

children.title: Checking at Once: Rav's Shiur Veset Condition
children.gist: Rav frees the other two only if she checked within the *shiur veset*, following Bar Padda's link between the husband's offering and pure foods, which R. Oshaya rejects.

bullets.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: the other two may attribute the blood to her only if she checked within the *shiur veset*, the brief time needed for bleeding to begin. If she checked later, she is impure and so are the others, out of doubt.
Rav follows Bar Padda.

children.title: Bar Padda: Three Time Spans, the Husband's Offering and Pure Foods
children.gist: Whatever the husband would owe after intercourse (*chatat*, *asham talui* or nothing), the pure foods she was preparing are impure, suspended or pure to match.

bullets.text: Three spans after intercourse: the *shiur veset*; the time to get out of bed and wash; and anything longer.
Where the husband would bring a *chatat* (blood within the *shiur veset*), the pure items she was preparing when she found blood are impure.
Where he would bring an *asham talui*, the pure items are suspended: they are neither burned nor eaten.
Where he would be exempt, the pure items remain pure.
Citing Rashi: the last span seems at odds with the rule of *me'et le'et*, which goes back a full day, from the opening of the tractate. The Gemara does not take this up here.

chart.caption: Bar Padda: the husband's offering and the woman's pure foods follow the same time spans
columns: Had it been intercourse, the husband
rows: Time to get out of bed and wash

children.title: R. Oshaya: What Held the Blood Back? The Child and Elder, the Finger in the Eye
children.gist: R. Oshaya breaks Bar Padda's link: only intercourse holds the blood back, as R. Yirmeya's and Abaye's parables show, so the pure foods remain only suspended.

bullets.text: R. Oshaya: there is no link. Even where the husband would bring a *chatat*, the pure items she touched are only suspended.
In intercourse the organ held the blood back, so she was already impure. While she was preparing food, what would have held it back?

R. Yirmeya's parable for R. Oshaya: a child and an old man on the road. On the road the child keeps the old man's pace; once they enter the city he runs ahead. So the blood comes quickly once intercourse ends.
Abaye's parable: as long as a man's finger is in his eye, the tears wait; once he removes it, they come at once.
That is what makes intercourse unique: a physical restraint explains why blood found right afterward was there during it. Elsewhere, blood found now is presumed to have appeared now.

children.title: Tolot Zo ba'Zo: Pregnant, Nursing, Old, Too Young
children.gist: The baraita pairs an unfit woman with a fit one: pregnant, nursing, old or not yet bleeding, each attributes to the other; if both share the same state, they are treated as fit and all are impure.

bullets.text: Baraita: one pregnant and one not: the pregnant woman attributes the blood to the one who is not pregnant.
Likewise nursing to not nursing; old (no longer bleeding regularly) to not old; and a virgin, here one who has not yet bled because of her youth, to one who has.
If both are pregnant, both nursing, both old or both virgins, it is as the Mishnah taught: they are treated as though fit to see, and all are impure.
The unfit woman is a less likely source of blood, so she may shift it onto the more likely one.

returns_to.note: Spells out the Mishnah's clause on attributing to each other

key_terms.definition: Assigning a blood stain to some other plausible source (another person, a wound, an outside cause) instead of to the woman who found it, so that she remains pure.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf asks to whom a stain may be attributed: a gentile who has or hasn't bled, a borrower who would lose less than the lender, a woman impure only by a stain, and one of several women in a bed.

key_terms.sense: a blood stain found without a felt flow
key_terms.definition: A blood stain a woman finds on her body, clothing or something she used, without having felt a flow. By rabbinic decree it can render her impure as a niddah, subject to set limits.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yochanan asks whether a stain may be attributed to a woman who is impure only because of a stain of her own; R. Yehuda bar Livai says no.

key_terms.definition: A woman who sees blood on one or two days outside her menstrual period. She must watch for one clean day and then immerse.
key_terms.on_this_daf: She is the paradigm borrower who would lose less than the lender. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows attributing a stain to her on her second day, Rebbi does not, and both allow it on her first day.

key_terms.sense: an object's susceptibility to ritual impurity
key_terms.definition: Whether an object can become ritually impure. Vessels and garments generally can; the ground, things fixed to it, stone objects and scraps too small to be useful cannot, and an earthenware vessel becomes impure only through its interior.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Nechemia holds that a stain on anything not susceptible to impurity does not make the woman impure, extended to a pot's exterior and to small rags, and the Sages ruled like him.

key_terms.definition: The period after childbirth, following the initial days of impurity, during which blood a woman sees does not make her impure by Torah law.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Attributing a stain to a woman in these days costs her nothing, so all agree it is allowed; Ravina reads the baraita's permitted case as such a woman.

key_terms.sense: the minimal time for bleeding to begin
key_terms.definition: The very short span of time it takes for bleeding to begin. Blood found within it is treated as present at the moment in question.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav: the other two women go free only if the one who found herself impure checked within this span; Bar Padda ties it to the husband's *chatat*.

judgment_calls: The first Mishnah and all its Gemara (Rav, the unequal-loss dispute, ketem be'ketem, R. Nechemia) are grouped under one top-level section on attribution; each could instead be its own top-level section. Chose the grouping so the headlines show them as parts of one Mishnah's discussion.
R. Yosei son of R. Chanina (s8) could be folded into the Rav Chisda–Rav Adda section; kept separate because it is a new ruling that decides between them, with a returns_to link.
Ravina's rereading (s12) could sit inside the baraita section (s11); kept as its own child because it returns to defend R. Yehuda bar Livai's answer, with a returns_to link to s10.
The scope starts at the Mishnah on 59b.19, although the Gemara's exchange begins at 59b.22, because Rav's comment and the whole daf depend on the Mishnah and the shiur teaches it here.
Bar Padda and R. Oshaya are nested under Rav's shiur veset condition because the Gemara brings them to explain Rav; they could be a separate top-level section on timing.
In the baraita resolutions, the first answer is labeled neutrally (not as R. Yochanan's), since the Sefaria translation's attribution to R. Yochanan is an interpolation of the anonymous Gemara.
coverage_notes: The Mishnah (59b.19–21) opens chapter 9; the previous shiur ended with chapter 8, so it is outlined here from this shiur.
The essay names Rav Papa as the one who reverses the reading of R. Meir; the text has Rava. Followed the text.
The essay has Rav Adda saying the impure traveler has a real but modest loss; the text has him say it makes no practical difference to the one already impure. Followed the text.
The essay omits that R. Yosei son of R. Chanina's ruling also covers an impure and a pure traveler and is said to follow Rav Adda, not Rav Chisda. Included from the text.
The essay attributes the answer 'she may not attribute' to Rebbi; the text gives it to R. Yehuda bar Livai. Followed the text.

The essay attributes the rereading of the baraita to Abaye and describes it as a gentile who had a stain; the text gives it to Ravina and speaks of the lender's status as one who saw a stain. Followed the text.

The essay explains Rav Ashi's past/future distinction (via Tosafot) as the timing of when the second stain was discovered; the text as translated speaks of pure items she already touched versus her future count. Followed the text for the Gemara bullet and kept only the lecturer's formal/evidentiary framing as a shiur bullet.
The essay says 'Darash R. Chiya bar Rav Mattana... Rav ruled publicly'; the text has Rav Chiyya bar Rav Mattana teaching in the name of Rav. Followed the text.
The essay calls the author of the restraint principle 'Rabbi Yoshia'; the text has R. Oshaya, and the parables of R. Yirmeya and Abaye explain his view. Followed the text.
The essay does not mention Bar Padda's middle span (time to get out of bed and wash); included from the text.
The essay's discussion of the three criteria of ketamim and the parallel to nega'im is shiur framing; the colored-garment criterion belongs to a later Mishnah and is only mentioned.
The essay's remark about women lying rigidly in the bed and the wall case belongs to 61a; left out except in 'continues'.
